Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

For a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$, a map
$$\tau:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$$
is a **stopping time** if $\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$. It is **bounded** if some deterministic $N$ satisfies $\tau\le N$ almost surely, and **finite** if $P(\tau<\infty)=1$. These notions are distinct: finite does not mean bounded.

The event condition is literal, not merely modulo null sets; no completion of the filtration is assumed. Measurability as an extended-integer-valued random variable follows from the equivalent event tests below.

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix any $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and define $\tau_\gamma=\inf\{t\ge0:E_t\ge1/\gamma\}$, with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$. For every $n$, $\{\tau_\gamma\le n\}=\bigcup_{k=0}^n\{E_k\ge1/\gamma\}\in\mathcal F_n$, so $\tau_\gamma$ is a stopping time. Also $\{\tau_\gamma\wedge N\le n\}=\{\tau_\gamma\le n\}$ for $n<N$ and is the whole space for $n\ge N$, so each $\tau_\gamma\wedge N$ is a bounded stopping time.

The constant time $0$ is a stopping time bounded by $0$, and step 1.1 shows $\tau_\gamma\wedge N$ is a bounded stopping time. Bounded optional sampling therefore gives $\mathbb E_P E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\le\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

On $\{\tau_\gamma\le N\}$, $E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\ge1/\gamma$; on its complement the stopped value is $E_N\ge0$ almost surely. Hence $\mathbb E_P E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\ge\gamma^{-1}P(\tau_\gamma\le N)$, and step 2.1 yields $P(\tau_\gamma\le N)\le\gamma$.

The events $\{\tau_\gamma\le N\}$ increase with $N$ and their union is $\{\tau_\gamma<\infty\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}\{E_t\ge1/\gamma\}$. Continuity from below and step 3.1 therefore give $P(\exists t\ge0:E_t\ge1/\gamma)\le\gamma$.

Let $H=\{\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge1/\alpha\}$ and suppose $q=P(H)>\alpha$. Since $q\le1$, $\beta=(\alpha+q)/2$ lies in $(\alpha,1)$, so $1/\beta<1/\alpha$. If every $E_t\le1/\beta$, then $\sup_tE_t\le1/\beta<1/\alpha$, contrary to $H$; hence $H\subseteq\{\exists t:E_t\ge1/\beta\}$ even if the supremum is not attained. Step 4.1 with $\gamma=\beta$ gives $q\le\beta<q$, a contradiction. Therefore $P(H)\le\alpha$, and since $P$ was arbitrary, the bound holds under every null law.

on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every

[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Fix $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $t\ge0$. For every $\lambda$, $P(E_t^\lambda\ge0)=1$, so $E_t^{\lambda,+}=E_t^\lambda$ $P$-almost surely and has the same expectation. Apply F3 at the deterministic times $0$ and $t$ to get $\mathbb E_P E_t^{\lambda,+}=\mathbb E_P E_t^\lambda\le\mathbb E_P E_0^\lambda=\mathbb E_P E_0^{\lambda,+}\le1$. The pointwise nonnegative map $(\lambda,\omega)\mapsto E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)$ is product-measurable; Tonelli F2 makes $\overline E_t$ $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and gives $\mathbb E_P\overline E_t=\int_\Lambda\mathbb E_P E_t^{\lambda,+}\,\pi(d\lambda)\le1$. Hence $N_t=\{\overline E_t=\infty\}\in\mathcal F_t$ is null under every $P\in\mathcal P_0$. The common modification $\widetilde E_t=\overline E_t$ off $N_t$ and $0$ on $N_t$ is finite, adapted, nonnegative and integrable under every null law, with $\mathbb E_P\widetilde E_0\le1$.

Fix $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $t\ge1$, and $A\in\mathcal F_{t-1}$. Since $E_s^{\lambda,+}=E_s^\lambda$ $P$-almost surely for $s=t-1,t$, the component supermartingale condition and the event-integral identity F5 give $\int_A E_t^{\lambda,+}\,dP=\int_A E_t^\lambda\,dP\le\int_A E_{t-1}^\lambda\,dP=\int_A E_{t-1}^{\lambda,+}\,dP$ for every $\lambda$. Tonelli F2 integrates these inequalities over $\pi$; since $N_t$ and $N_{t-1}$ are $P$-null, replacing the mixtures by $\widetilde E_t$ and $\widetilde E_{t-1}$ does not change these integrals. Thus $\int_A\widetilde E_t\,dP\le\int_A\widetilde E_{t-1}\,dP$.

Let $U=\mathbb E_P[\widetilde E_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, which exists by F4 and AC A1. For every $A\in\mathcal F_{t-1}$, the event-integral identity F5 and step 2.1 give $\int_A(U-\widetilde E_{t-1})\,dP\le0$. Take $A=\{U>\widetilde E_{t-1}\}$. If $P(A)>0$, then for some integer $m\ge1$ the subset where $U-\widetilde E_{t-1}\ge1/m$ has positive measure, making that integral strictly positive, a contradiction. Therefore $U\le\widetilde E_{t-1}$ almost surely. As $P$ and $t$ were arbitrary, $\widetilde E$ is a test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$.

Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common discrete filtered
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. A process
$p=(p_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **anytime-valid p-value process** for $\mathcal P_0$ if
each $p_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable with values in $[0,1]$ and, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P(\exists t\ge0:p_t\le\alpha)\le\alpha.$$

At time $t$, the rejection rule at threshold $\alpha$ is the
$\mathcal F_t$-measurable test function $\varphi_{t,\alpha}
=\mathbf 1_{\{p_t\le\alpha\}}$ in the sense of
[[def-randomized-test]]: the indicator supplies a binary probability kernel by
[[lem-measurable-rejection-function-defines-randomized-test]]. For any stopping time $\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$
[[def-discrete-stopping-time]], the rejection event is
$$\{\tau<\infty,\ p_\tau\le\alpha\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}\bigl(\{\tau=t\}\cap\{p_t\le\alpha\}\bigr).$$
For $t=0$, $\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le0\}\in\mathcal F_0$; for $t\ge1$,
$\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus\{\tau\le t-1\}\in\mathcal F_t$ by the
stopping-time condition and filtration property. Thus each term is in
$\mathcal F_t$, so this event is measurable and is contained
in the all-times crossing event; the definition therefore controls rejection
after data-dependent stopping.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common
discrete filtered measurable space and let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and
every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

derivations.claim: The map $g:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ defined by $g(x)=1$ for $x\le0$ and $g(x)=\min(1,1/x)$ for $x>0$ is Borel measurable. Thus $p_t=g(E_t)$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and $[0,1]$-valued. For $0<\alpha<1$, the threshold $1/\alpha>1$, so $p_t\le\alpha$ holds exactly when $E_t\ge1/\alpha$.

Taking the union over all $t$ in the equivalence of step 1.1 and applying F3 gives $P(\exists t\ge0:p_t\le\alpha)=P(\exists t\ge0:E_t\ge1/\alpha)\le P(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge1/\alpha)\le\alpha$ for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$. This is the defining anytime-valid condition.

For a fixed $t$ and $0<u<1$, $\{p_t\le u\}\subseteq\{\exists s:p_s\le u\}$, so its probability is at most $u$ by step 2.1. Since $E_t$ is finite, $p_t>0$; hence the bound at $u=0$ is zero, and at $u=1$ it is trivial. For any stopping time $\tau$, $\{\tau<\infty,\ p_\tau\le u\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}(\{\tau=t\}\cap\{p_t\le u\})$ is contained in the all-times crossing event for $0<u<1$; the endpoints follow as above. Thus fixed-time and stopping-time validity both hold.

If $\mathcal P_0$ is nonempty, form the fixed-time experiment with data space $(\Omega,\mathcal F_t)$, parameter set $\Theta=\mathcal P_0$, laws given by restriction to $\mathcal F_t$, and null set $\Theta_0=\Theta$. The observation is the identity map from the original sample space to this data space. Step 1.1 makes $p_t$ a statistic and step 3.1 gives its superuniform inequality under every law in $\Theta_0$, so F4 makes it a valid p-value in this experiment. If $\mathcal P_0$ is empty, all lawwise assertions are vacuous.
